import numpy as np, pandas as pd

PATH, LATE = "parcels.csv", "late"   # LATE = your late flag column (0/1)
K = 150                               # re-routes per day

# Yours to set before running:
TEST_DAYS = ... # how many of the most recent days to hold out (include a busy period if you can)
GAP_DAYS = ... # days dropped between train and test; at least the time a parcel takes to be delivered and flagged
SMOOTH = ... # group size you'd trust; smaller groups lean toward the overall rate
AREA_CHARS = ... # leading postcode characters that name the area
assert all(isinstance(v, int) for v in (TEST_DAYS, GAP_DAYS, SMOOTH, AREA_CHARS)), "set the four values above"

df = pd.read_csv(PATH, usecols=["parcel_id", "dispatch_time", "depot", "postcode", LATE],
                 parse_dates=["dispatch_time"])
df[LATE] = df[LATE].astype(int)
df["day"] = df["dispatch_time"].dt.normalize()
df["area"] = df["postcode"].astype(str).str.strip().str.upper().str[:AREA_CHARS]

# time split: oldest -> train, newest -> test, with a gap between
test_start = df["day"].max() - pd.Timedelta(days=TEST_DAYS)
train = df[df["day"] <= test_start - pd.Timedelta(days=GAP_DAYS)]
test = df[df["day"] > test_start].copy()

# baseline 1: same score for everyone (the overall late rate)
p0 = train[LATE].mean()
test["score_flat"] = p0

# baseline 2: past late rate of depot and postcode area, from train only
def rate_map(key):
    g = train.groupby(key)[LATE].agg(["sum", "count"])
    return (g["sum"] + SMOOTH * p0) / (g["count"] + SMOOTH)

for key in ["depot", "area"]:

test["score_rule"] = test[["depot_rate", "area_rate"]].mean(axis=1)

# evaluation: each day, take the K highest scores and count the truly late ones
test["tiebreak"] = np.random.default_rng().random(len(test))      # ties broken at random

def top_k(score):
    rows = []
    for _, g in test.groupby("day"):
        top = g.sort_values([score, "tiebreak"], ascending=False).head(K)
        rows.append((len(top), top[LATE].sum(), g[LATE].sum()))
    r = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["picked", "late_in_top", "late_total"])
    return r.late_in_top.sum() / r.picked.sum(), r.late_in_top.sum() / r.late_total.sum()

base = test[LATE].mean()
print("train late rate:", p0, "| test late rate:", base,

out = []
for name, col in [("overall rate", "score_flat"), ("depot+area rule", "score_rule")]:
    prec, rec = top_k(col)
    out.append({"score": name, "precision_at_K": prec, "share_of_late_caught": rec, "lift": prec / base})

Mostly attendance and grades, I think. Like how many kids come to school and how the grades are doing, by class. Not each child, just the classes.

transcript.text: Our on-time delivery rate fell from 94% to 88% after we introduced a new route plan in August. Operations wants to know whether to roll the plan back. I have the delivery logs but haven't sent them. How should we approach this?

Did the new route plan go live on every route at the same time, or did some routes or depots stay on the old plan? Did anything else change around August, such as volumes, drivers, depots or vehicles?

Good questions. On the rollout, I'm not sure whether every route switched on the same day or whether some depots stayed on the old plan. I'd have to check that against the route ids and dates in the logs. On other changes, I know August also brought holiday traffic and some new drivers. I don't know about volume, depot or vehicle changes, so I'd need to check those too. The logs run January to October and have delivery id, date, depot, route id, planned time, delivered time, a weather flag and driver id. That should let me compare routes on the old and new plan, and control for weather, drivers and depot. The director wants an answer in two weeks, so could you tell me the exact date the plan went live, and whether anyone recorded when each driver started? I'm happy to send the file once we agree on how to split it.

I can't tell you the go-live date or the driver start dates. Neither is in what you've described, and I don't want to guess. The go-live date should be in Operations' records, such as the route-planning change ticket or the rollout notice. Ask for it per depot or route, because that tells us whether any routes stayed on the old plan. Driver start dates would normally be with HR or dispatch. If nobody recorded them, each driver's first delivery in your logs is a rough stand-in, and it works well for drivers who started after January. You also don't need to plan a train/test split. This is a cause-and-effect question, not a prediction. What matters is who we compare with whom: routes on the new plan against routes still on the old one, and the same drivers and depots before and after. I've assumed "on time" means delivered at or before planned time, possibly with a grace window. Please tell me if your 94% and 88% use a different rule. Here are three ways we could go:

choices.title: Did the plan cause the drop? A before/after comparison
choices.what: DCLab compares on-time rates before and after the switch, route by route, and sets them against routes or depots still on the old plan, if there are any. It adjusts for weather, depot, and drivers (new versus experienced). It also shows how much of the drop the August holiday traffic and the new drivers could explain.

choices.title: A recommendation for Operations on rolling back
choices.what: DCLab builds the evidence above into a decision brief for Operations. It covers roll back everywhere, roll back only where the plan clearly hurt, or keep it and fix specific routes. It gives the case for each, what is still uncertain, and what a short test could settle.

choices.title: A dashboard to watch the rate by plan, depot and week
choices.what: DCLab sets up a dashboard of on-time rate by week, split by depot and old versus new plan, with weather and new-driver views. You can follow the effect of any rollback or partial change as it happens.

transcript.text: quick q: churn with 3% positives, should i report PR-AUC or ROC-AUC to my manager, and why? no data work, just the answer

Report PR-AUC as your headline number. Show ROC-AUC next to it only as a secondary figure. **Why PR-AUC**
- **ROC-AUC flatters you at 3% positives.** Its false-positive rate is divided by the huge pool of non-churners. A model can flag many non-churners, so most of its flagged customers are wrong, and still score a high ROC-AUC. - **PR-AUC tracks what your manager cares about.** It measures precision, meaning how many of the customers you flag really churn. It also measures recall, meaning how many of the churners you catch. That matches the real-world action of contacting the customers the model ranks highest. **How to present it**
- Always give the baseline. A random model's PR-AUC equals the share of positives, which for you is your 3%. Report your model's PR-AUC against that 3% line. A raw PR-AUC can look small to people used to ROC-AUC, and the comparison shows how much better than chance it is. - Add one concrete figure from the same ranking. Pick a contact budget your team could actually afford, such as the top slice of customers by risk. Then say what share of that slice are real churners and what share of all churners it catches. Managers usually grasp that better than any AUC. **Caveats**
- PR-AUC depends on the base rate, so don't compare it across datasets or periods with different churn rates. - ROC-AUC is still fine for saying how well the model ranks churners above non-churners in general. It just shouldn't be the number you lead with when positives are this rare. Does that cover what you need, or would you like help turning it into a line for your manager?
Mostly. I already know both metrics. Give me one or two plain sentences I can say to a non-technical manager on why we lead with PR-AUC. No jargon. Review is tomorrow.

Here are two sentences you can say as they are:

"Only about 3% of our customers leave, so many scores look good even when the 'at-risk' list is mostly wrong. We lead with this one because it shows how many of the customers we'd contact really were about to leave, and how many of the leavers we'd catch, compared with the 3% we'd hit by picking at random."

Do you want it cut to one sentence, or is this what you need for tomorrow?
That works, thanks. Show me what else you can do: a slide title and a one-line answer if he asks why we don't use ROC-AUC.

Here are both. **Slide title:** "Of the customers we flag as at risk, how many really leave?"

If you'd like a title that states the result, use: "Our at-risk list finds leavers far better than picking at random". Only use it once your own numbers back it up. **If he asks why we don't use ROC-AUC:** "That score is also fair, but when only 3% of customers leave it can look great even if the at-risk list is mostly wrong, so we lead with the score that shows how good the list really is."

Is that everything you need for tomorrow, or should I tighten any of these?
That's enough for tomorrow, thanks.
Glad that helps. Good luck with the review tomorrow!

Short answer: usually no, but it depends on one thing I can't see from the column list, so I'd rather not guess. Tenure is normally known before a customer leaves, so it's a fair input. It becomes leaky if it was measured after the outcome, for example if churned customers' tenure stops at their cancellation date while active customers' tenure runs to today. How was tenure_months calculated in your table: as of a fixed date before the month you're predicting, or up to the customer's last day or the export date?

I didn't build the pipeline, so I don't know offhand. Can you check it in the file? Compare tenure_months for churned_next_month = 1 vs 0 and see whether churned rows look capped at a cancellation date. I need to know by tomorrow whether to keep it.

Yes, I can check this in the file, and I'll do it as a comparison of tenure_months for churned_next_month = 1 vs 0. Your table also has signup_date, which gives a second test. If tenure_months matches the time from signup to one fixed date for every customer, it isn't capped at cancellation. If churned rows come out shorter, it is. I'm assuming you make the keep-or-drop call yourself tomorrow. Is that right, or is someone else, like a team building the churn model, relying on your answer?
Me. I make the keep/drop call and the feature list freezes tomorrow. Nobody else depends on it. Go ahead and run the check on the file I shared.

I've started the check on customers.csv. It has two parts:

1. **Churned vs. not churned.** DCLab will compare the distribution of tenure_months for churned_next_month = 1 against 0. If churned rows are capped at a cancellation date, they should look systematically shorter or bunch up in an odd way. 2. **Tenure against signup_date.** DCLab will test whether tenure_months matches the time from signup_date to one fixed date for every customer. If it does, tenure isn't capped at cancellation. If churned rows come out shorter than that fixed-date figure, tenure was measured up to the cancellation date, and that is leakage. You'll get the numbers from both comparisons, computed by DCLab's code, so you can make the keep-or-drop call before the list freezes tomorrow. I won't give you a verdict until those results are in. One caution for when you read them: churned customers can have a lower tenure without any leakage. Newer customers often churn more. That is why the signup_date test matters more than the group comparison.
